glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: God Himself appointed Jesus as High Priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, and through His prayers, suffering, and obedience He became the author of eternal salvation, yet the hearers have grown dull of hearing and need to grow up.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Hebrews 5 continues the teaching on Jesus’ priesthood that began at 4:14, measuring Him against the qualifications of Israel’s high priests descended from Aaron. At 5:11 the writer pauses for an appeal that runs through chapter 6 before he returns to Melchizedek in chapter 7.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• Hebrews 5:1–4 — Every High Priest Is Taken from Among Men

  • Hebrews 5:5–6 — God Appointed Christ as High Priest

  • Hebrews 5:7–10 — Perfected Through Suffering

  • Hebrews 5:11–14 — Dull of Hearing and in Need of Solid Food

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “though He was a Son, yet He learned obedience by the things which He suffered. And having been perfected, He became the author of eternal salvation to all who obey Him” (Hebrews 5:8–9)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Hebrews begins by describing every high priest from Aaron’s line. He was taken from among the people to represent them before God, offering gifts and sacrifices for sins. His own weakness helped him deal gently with those who went astray, though it also meant he had to offer sacrifices for his own sins. And no one could take that honor for himself; God had to call him, “just as Aaron was” (5:4).

Jesus meets both qualifications, in a greater way. He did not appoint Himself. The God who said, “You are My Son,” also said, “You are a priest forever According to the order of Melchizedek” (5:5–6). Nor is His sympathy borrowed from sin of His own, for He had none. “In the days of His flesh” He prayed “with vehement cries and tears to Him who was able to save Him from death” (5:7). The Father heard Him and brought Him through death and out of it. “Though He was a Son, yet He learned obedience by the things which He suffered” (5:8). He lived out obedience at real cost, and through it He reached the goal of His calling, becoming “the author of eternal salvation to all who obey Him” (5:9).

Then the writer stops. He has much to say about Melchizedek, but his hearers “have become dull of hearing” (5:11). By now they should be teaching others, yet they need the first principles again, like infants who still need milk. Solid food belongs to the mature, whose senses are trained by practice to tell good from evil (5:14).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Hebrews 5:1–4 — Every High Priest Is Taken from Among Men

Every high priest descended from Aaron was taken from among the people to represent them before God and offer sacrifices for sins. His own weakness helped him deal gently with the wayward but also required sacrifices for his own sins, and no one could take the office unless God called him.

Hebrews 5:5–6 — God Appointed Christ as High Priest

Christ did not take the honor of the high priesthood for Himself. God, who declared Him to be His Son, also appointed Him a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

Hebrews 5:7–10 — Perfected Through Suffering

During His earthly life Jesus prayed with loud cries and tears to the God who could save Him from death, and God heard Him because of His reverence. Though He was the Son, He learned obedience through suffering, and having reached the goal of His calling, He became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey Him.

Hebrews 5:11–14 — Dull of Hearing and in Need of Solid Food

The writer has much more to say about Melchizedek, but his hearers have become slow to listen. Instead of teaching others, they need the basics again, like infants on milk, while solid food belongs to the mature, who train their judgment by practice.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Hebrews 5 shows that Jesus’ priesthood rests on God’s appointment and on a real human life of costly obedience. He prayed with cries and tears, suffered, and obeyed to the end. That is why believers can trust Him: He did not escape the weight of human weakness, and God vindicated His obedience by raising Him (5:7–9).

The chapter also warns that believers can stop growing. The problem in 5:11–14 is not the difficulty of the subject but the hearers’ slowness to listen. Those who live only on milk remain unskilled in the word of righteousness, while the mature have their senses trained by practice to discern good from evil (5:13–14).

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Called by God. No high priest appoints himself. In Psalm 2 God declares Jesus His royal Son, and in Psalm 110 He appoints that Son a priest forever (5:4–6).

Compassion for the weak. A high priest deals gently with those who go astray, and Jesus knows human weakness without sin (5:2, 7–8).

Obedience through suffering. The Son learned obedience by what He suffered (5:7–8).

The author of eternal salvation. Jesus, perfected through suffering, is the source of lasting salvation (5:9).

Growing up. Dull hearing stalls growth, while practice trains discernment (5:11–14).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
High priest (5:1). The priest from Aaron’s line who represented Israel before God and offered sacrifices for sins, especially on the yearly Day of Atonement.

The order of Melchizedek (5:6, 10). A priesthood like that of Melchizedek, the king and priest of Salem who blessed Abraham (Genesis 14:18–20). God promised it in Psalm 110:4, and Hebrews explains it in chapter 7.

Heard because of His godly fear (5:7). God answered Jesus’ reverent prayer. In this context the answer is best seen in God bringing Him through death and raising Him from it (compare 13:20).

Perfected (5:9). Brought to the intended goal. Jesus was always without sin; through obedient suffering He completed His calling as Savior and High Priest.

Milk and solid food (5:12–14). Pictures of needing the basics taught again versus being ready to receive and use fuller teaching.

Senses exercised (5:14). Spiritual judgment trained through practice, the way a body grows strong through regular use.

focus: Hebrews 5 shows that Jesus meets the qualifications of a high priest, since God Himself appointed Him and He learned obedience through suffering, becoming the author of eternal salvation. The writer then pauses before explaining Melchizedek and rebukes hearers who have become dull of hearing and need the first principles taught again.

sections.title: Every High Priest Is Taken from Among Men
sections.summary: Every high priest is taken from among men and appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, and because he himself is subject to weakness, he can have compassion on the ignorant and those going astray, while for the same reason he must offer sacrifices for his own sins as well as for the people. No one takes this honor for himself; the high priest must be called by God, just as Aaron was.

sections.title: God Appointed Christ as High Priest
sections.summary: Christ did not glorify Himself to become High Priest; He was appointed by the One who said to Him, “You are My Son, Today I have begotten You” (Hebrews 5:5). In another place God declares, “You are a priest forever According to the order of Melchizedek” (Hebrews 5:6).

sections.title: Perfected Through Suffering
sections.summary: In the days of His flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications “with vehement cries and tears to Him who was able to save Him from death” (Hebrews 5:7), and He was heard because of His godly fear. Though He was a Son, He learned obedience by the things He suffered, and having been perfected He became the author of eternal salvation to all who obey Him, called by God as High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek.

sections.title: Dull of Hearing and in Need of Solid Food
sections.summary: The writer has much to say about Melchizedek that is hard to explain, because the hearers “have become dull of hearing” (Hebrews 5:11). Though they ought to be teachers by now, they need the first principles again, like infants who need milk, while solid food belongs to the mature, whose senses are trained by practice to discern both good and evil.

1.brief: Every high priest is taken from among men and appointed to act for them in matters relating to God, offering both gifts and sacrifices for sins. A high priest stands between God and the people and represents them before Him.
1.explain: “appointed for men in things pertaining to God” The high priest is chosen from the people and serves on their behalf before God. Gifts and sacrifices are part of that appointment because the people’s sins have to be dealt with. This describes the office before Hebrews explains how Jesus fills it.

2.brief: Because the high priest is himself subject to weakness, he “can have compassion on those who are ignorant and going astray.” His own frailty helps him deal gently with people who stumble.
2.explain: “He can have compassion” A priest’s own weakness gives him reason to deal gently with people who lack understanding or have wandered. Compassion here shapes the way he treats them as he represents them before God. Hebrews has already shown that Jesus understands temptation, and the next verse shows where the two priesthoods differ.

3.brief: Because of that same weakness, the high priest must offer sacrifices for his own sins as well as for the sins of the people. Aaron’s priesthood could not escape the priest’s own need for atonement.
3.explain: “so also for himself” The earlier high priest had sins of his own for which he had to offer sacrifice. On the Day of Atonement he brought an offering for himself and his household as well as the offering for the people (Leviticus 16:6, 15). This requirement helps explain why Jesus’ sinlessness matters to His priesthood.

4.brief: No one takes the honor of the high priesthood for himself; he must be called by God, “just as Aaron was.” The office is given by God’s appointment, not seized by human ambition.
4.explain: “he who is called by God” Priesthood is an honor God gives. Aaron received the office from God’s command in Exodus 28:1. The calling establishes the principle Hebrews applies to Jesus in the next two verses.

5.brief: In the same way Christ did not glorify Himself to become High Priest; He was appointed by God, who said to Him, “You are My Son, Today I have begotten You.” The God who declared Jesus to be His royal Son is the One who gave Him the honor of the priesthood.
5.explain: “Christ did not glorify Himself” Jesus received the honor of priesthood from the Father. The decree from Psalm 2:7 first identifies Him as God’s royal Son. The same God who speaks that decree also makes the priestly appointment in the next quotation.

6.brief: In another psalm God declares, “You are a priest forever According to the order of Melchizedek.” Psalm 110 joins God’s appointment to a priesthood that will never end, and Hebrews will later explain its connection to Melchizedek.
6.explain: “You are a priest forever” Psalm 110:4 adds the priestly declaration that Psalm 2 did not make. The Son has a permanent office according to the pattern of Melchizedek. The promise comes by God’s own word, and chapter 7 will explain why that pattern brings a priesthood greater than Aaron’s.

7.brief: In the days of His flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications “with vehement cries and tears to Him who was able to save Him from death,” and He was heard because of His godly fear. The Father answered His reverent prayer by bringing Him through death and raising Him from it.
7.explain: “with vehement cries and tears” During His earthly life Jesus prayed with real anguish to the Father, who could save Him from death. He was heard because of His reverent submission. The Father carried Him through suffering and answered by bringing Him out of death, as Hebrews 13:20 later says. His tears and His trust belonged to the same obedience.
7.notes: The expression rendered “save Him from death” can describe rescue out of death. The verse does not name the occasion of Jesus’ prayers. The language suits the anguish reported before the cross, while the statement that His prayer was heard reaches to the Father’s answer.

8.brief: Though Jesus was the Son, “yet He learned obedience by the things which He suffered.” The sinless Son came to know obedience by living it out at real cost in the midst of suffering.
8.explain: “He learned obedience by the things which He suffered” Sonship brings the cost of His obedience into relief. Jesus knew what obedience meant by living it through suffering. The sinless Son carried out His Father’s will when doing so involved real pain.

9.brief: Having been perfected, Jesus became “the author of eternal salvation to all who obey Him.” Through His obedient suffering He completed His saving calling, and He is now the source of lasting salvation for those who respond to Him in obedience.
9.explain: “the author of eternal salvation” Through obedient suffering Jesus reached the intended end of His saving work. As the One who completed it, He is the source of salvation that lasts forever. The people who receive it are described as obeying Him, a response of trust to the Savior who has done the saving.

10.brief: God has designated Jesus as High Priest “according to the order of Melchizedek.” The verse closes the comparison with Aaron by repeating the priesthood God promised in Psalm 110.
10.explain: “called by God as High Priest” God identifies the Son who was perfected through suffering as the High Priest promised in the order of Melchizedek. This brings the discussion back to Psalm 110:4 and sets up the explanation that resumes in chapter 7.

11.brief: The writer has much to say about Melchizedek, but it is hard to explain “since you have become dull of hearing.” The difficulty lies less in the subject than in hearers who have grown slow to listen.
11.explain: “you have become dull of hearing” The writer has more to say about the Melchizedek priesthood, but the congregation’s listening has grown sluggish. The problem developed over time. Before explaining the priesthood further, Hebrews addresses the kind of hearing that will let its teaching take hold.

12.brief: Though the hearers ought to be teachers by now, they need someone to teach them again “the first principles of the oracles of God,” and they have come to need milk rather than solid food. Their growth has stalled so badly that they need the basics retaught.
12.explain: “by this time you ought to be teachers” The hearers have had enough time to pass God’s teaching on to others. Instead, they need someone to teach them the first lessons of God’s word again. Milk and solid food picture the difference between needing to relearn those basics and being ready to receive fuller instruction.

13.brief: Everyone who lives only on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, “for he is a babe.” Remaining on spiritual milk leaves a believer inexperienced in using God’s teaching about what is right.
13.explain: “unskilled in the word of righteousness” A person who lives on milk is still an infant in the comparison. They lack experience in understanding and using the teaching that leads them in what is right. The verse explains why they have trouble taking in what the writer wants to teach.

14.brief: Solid food belongs to the mature, to “those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.” Maturity grows as believers put God’s word into practice and train their judgment through use.
14.explain: “by reason of use” Mature people become able to receive solid food because they have practiced what they learned. Practice trains their judgment to recognize both good and evil. This growth is the maturity the writer will urge his hearers to pursue in Hebrews 6:1.
